Hey everyone!

We are Atanas (@theatanas – Web Dev, UX/UI Designer, Artist & Actor) & Plamena (Designer & Web-Specialist), Timo (@treeck1 – AI Manager & Rhetoric/Storytelling Coach).

We are passionate about Moon & Mars exploration, coding, data visualization, AI, 3D, and storytelling!
summary:
Echonaut is an interactive space exploration website for young people ages 10–16 that brings the stories of NASA’s left-behind hardware to life. It responds to the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten” by turning NASA’s mission records and imagery into a curated, source-based story map.

Visitors spin and zoom into 3D globes of the Moon and Mars, select location markers, and discover the missions connected to each place. Mission pages combine approachable storytelling, images, maps, key figures, and selected audio narrations to explain why the equipment was sent, what it discovered, and what remains today. Information is based on NASA sources, and the pages show how certain the available data is. Echo, our friendly rover guide, accompanies the journey with helpful prompts and pop-up explanations of unfamiliar words and places. A “Beyond” section extends the adventure to selected missions beyond the Moon and Mars.

Rather than presenting an exhaustive catalogue, Echonaut connects a curated selection of missions with the questions and discoveries behind them. This matters because these machines are scientific and cultural heritage: their stories show how exploration builds on earlier missions and what we can learn from them. By making this knowledge accessible and engaging for young people, Echonaut turns hardware left far from Earth into a starting point for curiosity about science, engineering, and exploration, because a machine’s story does not end when it falls silent.
details:
They Went Silent. Their Echoes Didn’t.

What can a machine left on another world tell us about ourselves?

Echonaut is an interactive educational website that introduces young people ages 10–16 to NASA missions through the hardware they left behind. Our starting point is not a list of spacecraft specifications, but a set of questions: Why did we send it? What did it discover? Why did it stay? And where is it now?

We combine planetary exploration, mission storytelling, and a friendly rover guide to make those questions approachable. Instead of a catalogue of spacecraft, Echonaut offers a journey: young visitors zoom from a whole world to a single site, with a small rover companion helping them along the way. Our aim is to help young visitors connect the objects remaining far from Earth with the science, engineering, and human curiosity that took them there.

Explore a World, Find a Mission

The Moon and Mars sections feature interactive 3D globes that visitors can rotate and zoom into. Location markers connect places on each world with selected missions and the equipment associated with them.

Visitors can explore through the globe or browse the accompanying mission list. Selecting a location opens a card with information about the place and links to the related mission stories. This creates a journey from a whole world to a particular site—and from that site to the machines that explored it.

The experience also makes connections between missions visible. A single region can lead to more than one story, helping visitors understand exploration as a sequence of connected efforts rather than isolated events.

Discover What the Hardware Made Possible

Mission pages bring together readable explanations, imagery, location information, and key figures. They explain the mission’s purpose, its achievements, and the equipment that remained afterward.

For example, a visitor exploring the Moon can discover the Surveyor landers, locate their landing sites, and open a dedicated story about these robotic explorers. The page combines an introduction with mapped locations, mission status, numerical highlights, and an audio narration.

Maps can be enlarged for a closer look, while displayed coordinates connect the story to a specific place. Together, these elements help answer both “What happened?” and “Where did it happen?”

We use a curated selection of missions rather than attempting to include every mission researched. This keeps the experience focused on individual stories and gives visitors an approachable starting point for further exploration.

Meet Echo, Your Rover Guide

Echo is the small rover who accompanies visitors throughout the website.

The character provides contextual prompts, introduces discoveries, and explains unfamiliar terms and place names through pop-up explanations. Instead of asking learners to leave the story to look up a word, we bring the explanation to the point where they need it.

A name such as Oceanus Procellarum can therefore become a moment of discovery rather than a barrier to understanding. Echo helps connect unfamiliar scientific language with short, approachable explanations.

The character also gives the experience a consistent, welcoming presence across its different sections. Echo acts as a companion to exploration—not a replacement for the mission stories themselves. For some missions, a voice-over is also available that visitors can play and listen to.

Read, Listen, and Look Closer

Echonaut offers several ways into the same subject.

Visitors can explore locations visually, read mission stories, examine maps and images, or listen to narration on selected mission pages. Short numerical highlights provide another entry point into a mission’s scale and achievements.

These elements serve different purposes: the globe establishes location, the story supplies context, the figures highlight important details, and the audio offers an alternative way to follow the narrative.

The intended result is an experience that rewards curiosity without requiring prior knowledge of astronomy or spaceflight. Visitors get explanations exactly where they need them, and they can read, listen, or explore visually.

Beyond the Moon and Mars

The “Beyond” section extends the experience to selected missions farther afield, including Pioneer 10 and 11, NEAR Shoemaker, the Kepler Space Telescope, and Dawn.

These stories broaden the project beyond surface landing sites. They create opportunities to explore different mission purposes, destinations, and endings while retaining the same central questions: why the spacecraft went, what it contributed, and what happened afterward.

This section complements the Moon and Mars exploration without suggesting that every mission can be represented by a surface marker.

Technical and Content Approach

Echonaut connects an interactive geographic interface with structured mission content.

Its main experience components include:

  • Rotatable, zoomable 3D globes for the Moon and Mars.
  • Selectable location markers linked to mission information.
  • Mission lists and location cards that provide alternative navigation routes.
  • Dedicated story pages with imagery, mission information, and numerical highlights.
  • Expandable maps and displayed coordinates for geographic context.
  • Audio players on selected mission pages.
  • Contextual explanations and guidance delivered through Echo.

Behind this experience, our research foundation includes structured JSON mission records, GeoJSON location data, and JSON Schemas. These resources organize information about missions, equipment, locations, status, sources, and potential story material.

The website presents a selected subset of that broader research. The research collection and the published experience therefore serve different roles: one supports content development, while the other provides a focused journey for young visitors.


Design Decisions

We designed Echonaut around three factors: age-appropriate language for ages 10–16, source-based content drawn from NASA and scientific references, and clear limits on what is claimed. We deliberately chose a curated selection over completeness, and kept the mission stories at the centre while Echo supports them. Audio and visual elements offer alternative ways in for different learners.

Connecting the Hardware to Its Legacy

Echonaut responds to the challenge by making the equipment a starting point for understanding the exploration it enabled.

We do not want visitors to see only an abandoned lander or a silent spacecraft. We want them to understand the question it was built to answer, the discoveries it helped make, and the reasons it remained far from home.

Our intended impact is curiosity: encouraging young people to look at a marker on another world and ask what happened there—and why it still matters.
